title: Changes in spatio-temporal gait parameters and vertical speed during an extreme mountain ultra-marathon
authors: Jeker D, Falbriard M, Vernillo G, Meyer F, Savoldelli A, Degache F, Schena F, Aminian K, Millet GP
population: 27 runners with a shank inertial sensor on 10 mountain passes of a 220 km mountain ultra-marathon (low 1300-2000 m vs high 2400-3200 m)
findings: Average uphill vertical speed was 547 +/- 135 m/h, stride height 0.23 +/- 0.05 m and stride frequency 0.66 +/- 0.09 Hz.

There was a significant altitude x distance interaction on vertical speed (F(4,52) = 4.04, p < 0.01): early passes were faster at lower altitude, but the difference disappeared at a quarter of the race length.
The authors read this as neuromuscular fatigue influencing uphill velocity more than oxygen delivery.
The individual change in vertical speed correlated more strongly with change in stride height (r = 0.80, n = 321) than stride frequency (r = 0.43).
The authors suggest a large effect of knee extensor strength loss on the diminution of vertical speed.
limitations: Observational, 27 runners in one extreme race; altitude and distance covary; the mechanism is inferred from correlations. The abstract does not describe the runners' level.
implications: Use about 547 m/h (SD 135) as an observed mean uphill vertical speed in an extreme 220 km mountain ultra for the 27 runners studied; it is a ceiling-type reference for sustained climbing, not a race-average vert/h that includes flat and downhill sections. Expect decline with distance.
Plan knee-extensor strength work for long mountain events, since the fatigue-related loss of vertical speed was tied to shorter strides (a suggestion by the authors, from correlations).

verification.notes: Crossref: Eur J Sport Sci 20(10):1339-1345, 2020; Crossref lists nine authors (added Aminian K). PubMed PMID 31914356 abstract supports all numbers. Removed the unsupported 'recreational field' claim.
